summary:
The Jakarta Special Capital Region stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. In Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Raiding private gatherings is an established practice in the capital. Police arrested 141 people over a 'gay sex party' in Jakarta in May 2017, detained 144 at the Atlantis Gym sauna on 21 May 2017 with ten of them charged, and arrested 51 at a Central Jakarta sauna in October 2017 with six charged. The pattern resumed in 2025: 56 people were detained at a hotel in South Jakarta on 1 February, nine at another South Jakarta hotel on 24 May, and 75 people, 74 men and one woman, were arrested at a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor on 22 June after reports of a 'gay party'.

Amnesty International said the villa gathering violated no law, called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy, and observed that police made the arrests without naming detainees or conducting judicial proceedings. Those detained in that raid face up to 15 years' imprisonment under Indonesia's broadly worded Pornography Law.

No statute in Jakarta targets LGBT people directly. Police action rests on the 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction and on morality provisions; the 2006 law punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. Expression is restricted further: in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr.

Official hostility has moved into national security policy. An October 2025 presidential decree named the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture a non-military national security threat alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction. Reporting in August 2026 ties a surge in vigilante attacks on transgender people to that decree and to officials' public condemnations, and journalists describe a constant chilling effect, with editors killing LGBTQ+ stories out of fear of state reprisal or religious backlash.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.
tangentialFactors:
The capital's raids and Aceh's caning operate on different legal tracks. In Jakarta, detentions and charges are brought under the national pornography and morality provisions, whereas Aceh's caning is imposed under provincial religious law and reaches any foreign visitor present in that province.

Civil-society and independent media space has contracted since 2024-25, documented amid student-led anti-government protests. Editors report killing LGBTQ+ stories for fear of state reprisal or religious backlash, which narrows the reporting available on enforcement in the capital.

The October 2025 decree places LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy by listing them with terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction as non-military threats. Reporting published in August 2026 links that framing to a rise in vigilante attacks on transgender people.

A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025, adding a further layer to the existing pornography law and the 2016 broadcasting ban.
localsOnly:
In March 2018 the Jakarta Social Agency declared transgender waria 'socially dysfunctional' and detained trans women in city-run 'rehabilitation' centres unless they signed statements promising not to repeat their 'offence'.

Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option.

No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so residents have no general statutory claim when refused service, housing or employment.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the 22 June 2025 villa arrests is unresolved in the sources available here. The inventory records the arrests and Amnesty International's demand for release, but no charging decision, trial or release date for those 75 people.

Whether the 2025 bill on online content presenting LGBT behaviour has been enacted is not sourced. It is recorded as under discussion during 2025.

The provincial position on anti-discrimination or public-order regulation covering gender identity in Jakarta is not sourced. The absence of a national anti-discrimination statute is documented; whether the capital region has its own instrument is unresolved.

Enforcement figures for the penal code provisions in force from 2 January 2026 are not available for this jurisdiction. Reporting describes prosecutions as selective rather than systematic without case counts for the capital.

The final disposition of the 2017 sauna and party cases, and of the 2015-era detentions beyond the charges noted, is not sourced.
